head: c8cb37a
target: Judge a run from its run log: engine invariants, where one failing run is a bug, model behaviors, measured as rates over the trials that had the chance, and cost, reported but never judged.
incidental: the exact token sums and ratios of the cost report
the small helpers: the JSON string walker, the argument and pattern matchers, the tests' evidence picker
the test fixtures: the faux model, the canary secret, the weather, clock and guard plugins
the parsing of each transcript message shape into the run view

questions.prompt: Before this change, the live test asserted a few properties by hand and logged the rest. Why does the report split its verdicts into invariants and behaviors?

options.label: An invariant failure is an engine bug, and a behavior failure is data about the model.
Behaviors can fail safely, but an invariant failure stops the report from being written at all.
Invariants read the transcript, behaviors read the event stream, so the two need different judges.
A behavior failure becomes an engine bug once it repeats across many runs, so the split is bookkeeping.

key_points: Mixed together, an engine bug and a model mistake look alike, and each gets the wrong response.
One failing run proves an engine bug, so an invariant never waits for a rate.
A behavior is a bet on the model, judged per trial and read as a rate.
Cost is reported and never judged.

questions.prompt: The judge takes only the run log as its input. What does that boundary buy?

options.label: The live test, the CLI and the future grader all read the same files and get the same verdict.
Reading files is faster than keeping a whole run in memory.
A live judge would see unredacted events, so only the files are safe to read.

key_points: Any caller gets the same verdict from the same files: the live test, the CLI, the grader.
The grader judges runs it never saw happen, from the files alone.

questions.prompt: A behavior skips when the run never gave the model the chance to show it. What breaks if a skip counts as a failure?

options.label: Rates would punish runs that gave no chance, and runs in different modes or scenarios would stop comparing.
Nothing breaks: the model still failed to show the behavior, so the rate should fall.
Skips would hide real model failures, because the report could no longer tell them apart.
The engine would log an invariant failure, because a skip and a failure are one kind.

key_points: A rate counts only the trials that had the chance to show the behavior.
A skip says the run gave no chance; it is not a loss by the model.
Native-mode runs never show dispatch recovery, so counting skips there would read as model failure.

questions.prompt: The grader will rate one behavior across many runs of the same scenario. What does it key each verdict on, and why is that key unique?

options.label: The behavior's name and its step number; the scenario allows one expectation of each check per step.
The turn the behavior was judged in, which every run reaches in the same order.
The tool the behavior names, which is unique within the plugin set.
The prompt's text, hashed, so runs compare on what the model was asked.

key_points: Each verdict carries the behavior's name joined with its step number.
The scenario refuses a second expectation of the same check on one step, so keys stay unique.

questions.prompt: The judges read the transcript and the event stream together. Name the two cases where the event stream alone would misjudge a run.
key_points: No listener sees the records a session writes when it is created, so the plugins enabled at start come from the transcript.
In dispatch mode, a tool call rejected on its schema leaves no tool event, only an error result in the transcript.

questions.prompt: A new engine property joins the invariants. Which of these are true?

options.label: The build fails until its test table carries both a passing case and a failing case.
The report gains a key for it, derived from the table that lists the invariants.
It skips on runs that never used the plugin it is about.
Scenarios must declare it on every prompt step, or the run skips it.

key_points: The invariants table is the list; the report's keys and the type come from it.
The test tables are typed by the check names, so a check without cases does not compile.
An invariant is judged on every run, never skips, and needs no declaration in the scenario.

questions.prompt: A three-step run stops: the prompt of step 2 ends aborted mid-answer. What does the report say about the run, the invariants, and the behaviors of steps 2 and 3?
key_points: The report marks the run incomplete, because not every scenario step ran.
The invariants are still judged on the steps that ran.
The behaviors of step 2 skip, because its prompt never finished.
The behaviors of step 3 skip, because the run never reached them.
